# Title and abstract

## Working title

**Exponential Random Graph Models as a Benchmark for Directed Link and Hyperlink Prediction under Missingness**

## Abstract

Directed interaction data can be evaluated at several non-equivalent levels: the
dyadic arcs induced by records, algebraically derived directed groups, and the
recorded ordered groups themselves. We develop a missingness-centred benchmark
that keeps these targets separate and compares directed link-prediction scores
with conditional scores from a directed exponential random graph model (ERGM).
The primary design uses event-first masking of ordered tail/head event types on
a strict Enron custodian core and a reconstructed MathOverflow interaction core.
Each dataset has 30 fixed masks under MCAR and activity-biased MNAR-out
missingness. Random arity-matched panels, directional hard panels, and fixed
role-assignment tasks distinguish footprint completion from recovery of event
orientation. On random native-event panels, the predeclared `M4c::L1g` ERGM
conditional-footprint score exceeded the density reference `M0::L1` in PR-AUC
by 0.3584 (95% bootstrap interval 0.3519–0.3648) and 0.3324
(0.3269–0.3379) for Enron under MCAR and MNAR-out, and by 0.2396
(0.2305–0.2485) and 0.2394 (0.2303–0.2484) for MathOverflow. These are
within-network, matched-mask comparisons. Formal concepts did not exactly match
any native-event type in either core, despite footprint Jaccards of 0.8567
(Enron) and 0.6634 (MathOverflow). Thus, good dyadic-footprint completion does
not establish recovery of an observed directed group. The paper reports a
bounded chronological diagnostic but does not claim forecasting, a neural
benchmark, or an MCMC-derived higher-order joint ERGM result.

**Keywords:** directed networks; hyperlink prediction; exponential random graph
models; network missingness; formal concepts; native events

# Introduction

A missing directed interaction can be interpreted in more than one way. At the
most familiar level, the task is to rank absent dyads in an observed graph.
Classical link prediction treats this as a topology-based ranking problem and
uses proximity measures such as common neighbours and Adamic-Adar [1]. But many
directed records are not inherently dyadic. An email has a sender and a recipient
set; a question-answering exchange can have a set of answerers and one asker. If
such records are aggregated into directed arcs, the aggregate preserves some
footprints of an event while discarding much of its group and role identity.

This paper studies that distinction under missingness. It asks how directed link
prediction, directed hyperlink prediction, and ERGM conditional scores relate
when the intended target is made explicit. The problem is not to introduce a
new universal predictor. It is to build a reproducible benchmark that stops a
strong dyadic result from being misread as recovery of an observed directed
group.

ERGMs provide a useful statistical comparator because their conditional tie
probabilities are functions of model change statistics with the rest of the
network held fixed [2]. This makes it possible to compare a local directed score
with an ERGM conditional score on the same masked graph. It does not imply that
an MPLE fit supplies a joint probability for a multi-dyad event footprint.
Jointness requires an additional conditioning and simulation argument, whose
feasibility must be demonstrated rather than presumed.

The paper also distinguishes recorded groups from formal concepts. In formal
concept analysis, derivation operators identify closure pairs in a binary
relation [3]. Applied to a directed aggregate graph, these pairs yield
maximal tail/head structures and are legitimate structural targets. They are
not automatically the recorded events that generated the relation. The empirical
fidelity audit in this paper makes that non-identifiability visible rather than
assuming it away.

The project continues the missingness-centred comparison of LP, HP, and ERGM
estimation in the author's accepted undirected-network study. Direction changes
both the data-generating record and the evaluation problem: tails and heads have
different roles, missingness can target outgoing activity, and a reversal or
role-exchange negative can be much harder than a random non-event. The primary
analysis therefore uses event-first masks and reports random, hard, and
role-assignment evaluations separately.

The contribution is fourfold. First, the benchmark formalizes a target ladder
among dyadic footprints, formal concepts, and native events. Second, it compares
directed heuristics and split-specific ERGM conditional-footprint scores under
the same frozen missingness realizations. Third, it shows why strong footprint
overlap and random-panel ranking do not by themselves identify a recorded group
or its tail/head roles. Fourth, it preserves a narrow chronological diagnostic
without recasting the paper as a forecasting contest.

That last boundary matters. Models designed for time-ordered polyadic events,
such as relational hyperevent models, directly represent a sender and a receiver
set and are appropriate competitors for a full event-forecasting study [4].
Such a study would require rolling origins, a forecasting horizon, and a
formation/persistence design. Those choices belong to the planned second paper.
Here the contribution remains a static missingness benchmark with a bounded
temporal check.

# Targets and score logic

## From events to footprints and concepts

For an observed directed relation \(D=(V,A)\), a native event is an ordered
pair \(e=(T,H)\), where \(T\) and \(H\) are non-empty, disjoint actor sets.
Its directed two-section footprint is

\[
\pi(e)=T\times H.
\]

If \(\mathcal E\) is an event collection, aggregation yields
\(A=\bigcup_{e\in\mathcal E}\pi(e)\). This map is many-to-one. Distinct event
collections can induce the same directed graph, and a graph alone cannot
generally identify which event collection produced it.

Formal concepts offer one reproducible structural section of the aggregate
relation. For \(X,Y\subseteq V\), define common successors and predecessors
by

\[
X^{\uparrow}=\{v:(x,v)\in A\ \text{for every }x\in X\},\qquad
Y^{\downarrow}=\{u:(u,y)\in A\ \text{for every }y\in Y\}.
\]

A formal concept is a fixed pair \((T,H)\) with
\(T^{\uparrow}=H\) and \(H^{\downarrow}=T\). Equivalently, it is a maximal
complete tail-head rectangle in the adjacency relation. It is a property of the
aggregate graph, whereas a native event is a property of the record stream. The
benchmark therefore evaluates the two targets separately.

## Directed local scores and an ERGM conditional score

Let \(N^+(i)\) and \(N^-(i)\) denote the observed successors and predecessors
of actor \(i\). The three directed common-neighbour components used in the
benchmark are

\[
 s^{OI}_{ij}=|N^+(i)\cap N^-(j)|,\qquad
 s^{OO}_{ij}=|N^+(i)\cap N^+(j)|,\qquad
 s^{II}_{ij}=|N^-(i)\cap N^-(j)|,
\]

with total \(s^{CN}_{ij}=s^{OI}_{ij}+s^{OO}_{ij}+s^{II}_{ij}\). The same
roles are used by the directed Adamic-Adar variants, with each common neighbour
weighted by its observed total degree.

For a transitive-triple statistic that counts ordered triples
\(a\to b\to c\) with shortcut \(a\to c\), toggling arc \(i\to j\) changes the
statistic by \(s^{CN}_{ij}\). The new arc can act as the shortcut, the first
leg, or the second leg, yielding the OI, OO, and II terms respectively. Thus an
ERGM containing only an edge term and this transitive-triple statistic has a
conditional log-odds that is an affine function of total directed common
neighbours. This is an arc-level relationship. It does not imply that a lifted
higher-order candidate score is identical across methods.

For an ERGM with statistic vector \(g(Y)\), the conditional tie score is

\[
 p_{ij}=\Pr_\theta(Y_{ij}=1\mid Y_{-ij})
 =\operatorname{logit}^{-1}\{\theta^\top\Delta_{ij}g(Y)\}.
\]

In this paper, \(p_{ij}\) is estimated through the split-specific MPLE fit and
used as a conditional score. It is not presented as an MCMC-validated marginal
probability.

## Footprint aggregation and the dependence boundary

For a candidate \(e=(T,H)\), define three score summaries over its footprint:

\[
L_1(e)=\frac{1}{|T||H|}\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{h\in H}p_{th},\qquad
L_{1g}(e)=\left(\prod_{t\in T}\prod_{h\in H}p_{th}\right)^{1/(|T||H|)},
\]

and the factorized product

\[
L_2^{\mathrm{fac}}(e)=\prod_{t\in T}\prod_{h\in H}p_{th}.
\]

`L1` is an arithmetic footprint average and `L1g` is a size-normalized
geometric average. The factorized product is sensitive to footprint size. None
of these quantities is automatically the probability that all footprint arcs
are present jointly. A joint quantity would require all unknown candidate arcs
to be placed under a shared observation constraint and evaluated from the
corresponding joint conditional distribution.

This distinction sets the dependence boundary of the paper. The primary results
use `L1`, `L1g`, and factorized `L2` as conditional-pseudolikelihood score
constructions. A successful MCMC-derived higher-order joint score is not
available for the primary Enron model ladder. The manuscript consequently does
not use an observed gap between `L2` and a simulation score as a substantive
primary dependence estimate.

## Bounded temporal implication

When every temporal predictor is a function only of a previous network window,
the resulting next-window dyad scores factorize conditional on that history.
Within-window dependence enters only when terms are evaluated on the response
window itself. This paper uses that observation to organize a bounded
history-versus-contemporaneous diagnostic. It does not convert the benchmark
into a native-event forecasting analysis.

# Data, targets, and benchmark design

## Target ladder

Let a directed relation be \(D=(V,A)\), where \(A\subseteq V\times V\)
contains no loops. A recorded directed group event is an ordered pair
\(e=(T,H)\) of non-empty, disjoint actor sets: the actors in \(T\) occupy the
tail role and those in \(H\) occupy the head role. Its dyadic footprint is
\(T\times H\). Aggregating records gives the directed graph whose arc set is
the union of their footprints.

The benchmark keeps three targets distinct. **Arc prediction** concerns a
missing dyad. **Native-event prediction** concerns a recorded ordered tail/head
event type. **Formal-concept prediction** concerns a maximal tail/head pair
derived from the aggregate relation by the predecessor-successor Galois
connection. A formal concept can have a footprint that largely agrees with
recorded-event footprints without being the same ordered group. This distinction
is empirical rather than merely terminological: Table 2 reports zero exact
concept/event matches in both primary native-event cores.

We enumerate concepts cap-first, retaining only pairs with \(|T|\leq 3\) and
\(|H|\leq 3\). The cap is an explicit representation and computing boundary.
It is not a claim that the retained concepts are all observed groups, and it is
not applied after an unbounded enumeration.

## Data eligibility and privacy

Table 1 records the study's dataset eligibility decisions. The primary
native-event analyses use two 100-node cores. The Enron core is a conservative
internal-custodian benchmark: it retains only complete records whose sender and
all To/Cc recipients have approved custodian mappings in the 1998–2002 interval.
It has 7,820 retained events and 635 static directed arcs. This is not a claim
to represent the complete Enron communication system.

The MathOverflow core represents a different role structure. A native event is
a declared-window set of distinct answerers in the tail and the question asker
in the head. Its reconstruction policy, including the answer window and
handling rules, is frozen before the benchmark. It is therefore a reconstructed
native-event target, not an email analogue.

EU-core is retained for a bounded directed-dyadic chronological diagnostic.
CAVIAR is retained only as a full static directed-matrix, dyadic/footprint
analysis. Ciel lacks source-specific direction evidence, and Jmail remains
admissibility-pending; neither contributes a substantive result. All manuscript
inputs are aggregate-only. Raw archives, email content, email addresses,
identity maps, candidate-level scores, and per-event predictions are excluded.

## Missingness design

The primary unit of missingness is a distinct ordered tail/head native-event
type. When a type is selected, every repeated record of that type is withheld,
and the observed graph is rebuilt from the remaining types. Thus an observed
footprint of a held-out event is not leakage: a different observed event type
may induce the same dyads.

For each native-event core, the primary analysis fixes 30 MCAR masks and 30
MNAR-out masks at nominal type-level rate 0.30. MCAR uses fixed-count sampling.
MNAR-out is the predeclared oracle inclusion mechanism that favours types
associated with high-activity senders; its realised type rate can therefore vary
slightly. Because the same nominal type rate can remove different numbers of
records and projection arcs, all mask descriptions retain type-, record-, and
arc-level realised loss. MNAR-in and the rate grid are supplementary analyses,
not a replacement for the two primary mechanisms.

## Candidate panels and evaluation tasks

The random native-event panel contains held-out types and true non-event
negatives matched exactly on tail and head arity. Candidate participants must
be within weak distance two in the split-specific observed projection. Observed
and held-out event types are excluded from the negative pool. The random panel
therefore evaluates ranking in a defined, balanced, arity-matched
case-control universe; its PR-AUC is not a calibrated probability at natural
prevalence.

Two hard panels impose directional alternatives. The reversal/orientation panel
compares \((T,H)\) with its unobserved reversal \((H,T)\). The role-exchange
panel swaps one tail actor and one head actor while preserving the actor set and
both role arities. A fixed-role-assignment task provides the known participants
and the true arities, then asks the score to rank compatible role partitions.
No unavailable hard case is replaced by an easier random negative.

## Directed scores and ERGM benchmark

The heuristic branch lifts dyadic directed scores over a candidate footprint.
It includes reverse-arc, degree-product, directed common-neighbour, and
Adamic-Adar components. These are uncalibrated rankings, so the native-event
analysis reports ranking metrics rather than accuracy, F1, or log loss.

For each frozen split, the ERGM branch fits the designated directed static
specifications only to the observed projection using MPLE. The reported
single-dyad values are exact conditional pseudolikelihood scores under the
fitted model. Candidate footprints are summarized by `L1` (arithmetic mean),
`L1g` (geometric mean), and factorized `L2` (product). These are not the same
object as a jointly simulated footprint probability. In particular, the
factorized `L2` does not impose one shared observation constraint on every
unknown candidate dyad.

The predeclared primary ERGM comparison is `M4c::L1g` against `M0::L1` on the
random native-event panel. `M0` is the density reference. `M4c` adds directed
mutuality, degree, closure, and cyclic structure in the stated MPLE ladder. The
comparison tests conditional-score discrimination in the frozen-mask candidate
panel; it does not estimate an event-generating probability or establish ERGM
coefficient inference.

## Paired uncertainty and chronological boundary

For the primary 30-mask branches, uncertainty is calculated by resampling whole
frozen masks within dataset: 10,000 percentile-bootstrap draws give 95%
intervals, and 20,000 paired sign-flip draws give two-sided reference
contrasts. Mask replicates are not treated as independent networks, and no
cross-network pooling is performed.

The temporal work is restricted to a chronological diagnostic on Enron and
EU-core. Factorized lagged score models and a small btergm MPLE ladder compare
history-only and history-plus-contemporaneous specifications over two response
transitions. They do not provide a rolling-origin forecast evaluation, a joint
temporal probability, or a STERGM/RHEM comparison. Those questions are
explicitly deferred to the separate forecasting paper.

# Results

## Formal concepts preserve footprints without recovering recorded events

The cap-first concept sections have different coverage profiles in the two
primary cores. Enron contains 232 capped formal concepts over 635 static arcs;
MathOverflow contains 207 over 1,020 arcs. The critical comparison is not the
number of concepts but their relation to recorded group events (Table 2).

Neither core contains an exact tail/head match between a capped formal concept
and a native-event type. Concept precision and native-event-type recall are both
zero. Yet the footprint Jaccard is 0.8567 in Enron and 0.6634 in MathOverflow.
In Enron, concepts cover 86.62% of the native-event footprint arcs, while native
events cover 98.73% of the concept footprint arcs. The corresponding quantities
for MathOverflow are 66.47% and 99.70%.

This contrast is central to the benchmark. The aggregate graph retains enough
shared dyadic structure for a concept section to overlap strongly with event
footprints, but it does not identify the observed ordered group. Concept
recovery and native-event recovery are therefore reported as different targets.
The result does not license the interpretation of a formal concept as a
reconstructed email or question-answering event.

## Random native-event panels show conditional-score gains

Table 3A reports selected predeclared random-panel rows from 30 frozen masks
per dataset and primary missingness mechanism. The constant-density ERGM
reference `M0::L1` has PR-AUC 0.5000 on every balanced random panel. The
higher-order conditional-footprint score `M4c::L1g` reaches 0.8584 and 0.8324
in the Enron MCAR and MNAR-out panels, and 0.7396 and 0.7394 in the
MathOverflow MCAR and MNAR-out panels.

The directed heuristic patterns differ across the two interaction settings. In
Enron, total directed Adamic-Adar has PR-AUC 0.7966 under MCAR, whereas the
reverse-arc mean is stronger under MNAR-out (0.7761 versus 0.7472). In
MathOverflow, total directed Adamic-Adar has PR-AUC 0.7589 under MCAR and
0.7593 under MNAR-out, while the reverse-arc score is near the balanced-panel
reference. These results are descriptive comparisons of fixed, arity-matched
candidate panels rather than calibrated prevalence claims.

The predeclared paired ERGM contrast confirms the random-panel separation
within each fixed network (Table 4). Relative to `M0::L1`, `M4c::L1g` raises
PR-AUC by 0.3584 in Enron under MCAR (95% percentile-bootstrap interval
0.3519–0.3648) and 0.3324 under MNAR-out (0.3269–0.3379). The corresponding
MathOverflow differences are 0.2396 (0.2305–0.2485) and 0.2394
(0.2303–0.2484). Every paired sign-flip calculation attains the 20,000-draw
Monte Carlo lower resolution, 1/20,001. These intervals and p-values quantify
variation across the 30 frozen missingness realizations in a fixed dataset; they
are not cross-network or population inference.

## Directional hard panels qualify random-panel conclusions

The hard panels hold the actor set or an oriented alternative much closer to the
positive than the random panel does (Table 3B). Therefore they test a different
claim: whether scores retain information about a directed event's roles after
simple footprint completion is no longer sufficient.

In Enron, the `M4c::L1g` PR-AUC is near the balanced reference under MCAR for
both reversal/orientation (0.4899) and role exchange (0.4969). Under MNAR-out,
the same score rises modestly to 0.5575 and 0.5423, and the reverse-arc mean is
similarly directional (0.5685 and 0.5515). Thus the Enron random-panel lift
does not transfer to a stable directional-event recovery result.

MathOverflow has a different hard-panel profile: `M4c::L1g` is above the
balanced reference in both mechanisms and both panels, ranging from 0.6115 to
0.6543. However, its score level and the heuristic ordering are target- and
dataset-specific, rather than uniform consequences of random-panel performance.
The evidence supports the narrower conclusion that a directional test can alter
both performance level and ordering. It does not justify a single model as a
universal role-recovery method.

The role-assignment results reinforce this distinction (Table 3C). With the
participants and role arities supplied, Enron's reverse-arc mean has weighted
top-1 accuracy 0.6012 under MCAR and 0.6541 under MNAR-out, while MathOverflow
is better ranked by degree-product mean (0.7817 and 0.7521). The role task does
not use random case-control prevalence and is not interchangeable with the
random or hard panel metrics.

## The chronological analysis remains a bounded diagnostic

Table 5 records the status of the temporal checks. In both Enron and EU-core,
all three factorized lagged models completed over two response transitions. The
small btergm MPLE ladder completed through `T1` for Enron, while its
contemporaneous `T2` and `T2_minus_H` specifications had non-finite
coefficients. The EU-core btergm branch produced finite statuses for the
listed models, still using only two response panels and 20 bootstrap
replicates.

These outputs make the intended conceptual distinction observable: a lagged
score is conditional on history, whereas a contemporaneous conditional score
uses within-window structure. They do not yield a same-design forecast contest,
temporal simulation result, or evidence about formation and dissolution.
Accordingly, the chronological material is retained as a diagnostic and not
used to enlarge the paper's central missingness claim.

## Explicit exclusions protect the claim boundary

Table 6 records the gates that constrained the final evidence set. Higher-order
MCMC estimation did not satisfy the Enron feasibility gate, so there is no
primary MCMC-derived joint `L3` result. The official NHP-D reproduction gate
did not supply a defensible directed neural benchmark. Regime K,
masking-plus-forecasting, STERGM, RHEM, and rolling-origin native-event
forecasting are outside this paper. These are substantive scope controls rather
than unreported negative results.

# Discussion

The central result of this benchmark is a target distinction. A directed graph
constructed from interaction records can be informative for the dyadic
footprints of those records without retaining the records themselves. The Enron
fidelity audit makes the distinction unusually sharp: its capped formal concepts
have high footprint agreement with the native-event projection but zero exact
tail/head matches with native event types. MathOverflow shows the same
non-identity with lower footprint overlap. A formal concept should therefore be
reported as a structural object derived from an aggregate relation, not as a
recovered email or question-answering group.

Within the stated random native-event panels, higher-order ERGM conditional
footprint scores substantially improve on the density reference. The paired
results make this claim stronger than a single pilot split: the `M4c::L1g −
M0::L1` PR-AUC difference is positive in every primary data-mechanism cell, with
narrow percentile intervals over the 30 frozen masks. The claim is nevertheless
narrow. It concerns variation induced by repeated masking of one fixed network
under a fixed candidate universe. It is not evidence for a population effect,
for common performance across networks, or for calibrated probabilities of
natural event occurrence.

The hard panels clarify why this qualification matters. A random negative
matched by arity can differ from the positive in actors, roles, and footprint
structure. A reversal or role-exchange negative preserves far more of that
structure. In Enron, the random-panel ERGM advantage is near the balanced
reference under MCAR hard panels, whereas MathOverflow retains some directional
separation. Role assignment also changes the ordering of heuristic components
between the two datasets. These contrasts are not a failure of the random-panel
benchmark. They show that footprint completion and role recovery answer
different questions and should not be combined into one score claim.

Several limitations are substantive. The Enron core is deliberately conservative
because it retains only complete events within an approved internal-custodian
mapping. The MathOverflow events depend on a fixed reconstruction policy. Both
primary benchmarks use 100-node cores and a cap of three for tail and head
arity. Candidate panels are balanced and constrained by the observed
projection. MNAR-out uses oracle full-data activity to construct a stress test,
so it is not an observational estimate of an unknown real missingness process.

The ERGM interpretation is also restricted. The displayed scores are MPLE-based
conditional pseudolikelihood quantities. The factorized footprint summaries do
not become joint event probabilities merely because multiple dyad scores are
combined. The Enron higher-order MCMC feasibility gate did not converge or mix
within the predeclared bounded policy, so this paper does not report an
MCMC-derived `L3` dependence result. The M4 parameter-plug-in joint calculation
is retained only as a labelled supplementary score-mechanics sensitivity.

The chronological analysis should be read with the same restraint. It documents
that history-only and contemporaneous conditional-score specifications are
conceptually different and records which small MPLE branches were numerically
available. It does not evaluate future-event forecasts. A full temporal paper
will instead use rolling origins, native-event targets, TERGM/conditional STERGM
specifications where justified, and relational hyperevent models as event-level
competitors.

## Conclusion

A directed missingness benchmark must specify what has gone missing. Dyadic
footprints, formal concepts, and recorded tail/head events are related but
non-interchangeable targets. On the two primary native-event cores, ERGM
conditional footprint scores rank random held-out event types well relative to
a density reference, but those gains do not collapse the distinction between
footprint completion and recovery of a directed group. Reporting random, hard,
and role-specific tasks separately makes that boundary empirical rather than
rhetorical. The resulting framework is reproducible, explicit about failed
feasibility and reproduction gates, and deliberately leaves forecasting to the
separate temporal event-prediction study.

## Table 06 Pilot Gates And Exclusions

Compact transcription of the Phase 2 completion review. It preserves negative gates as explicit methodological evidence.

| gate | status | consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Data provenance and target eligibility | Passed with scope restrictions | Enron and MathOverflow support native-event targets; EU-core is temporal dyadic; CAVIAR is static full-matrix only. |
| Target representation | Passed as diagnostic | Formal concepts remain a derived target distinct from recorded events. |
| Higher-order ERGM MCMC feasibility | Not passed for primary claim | No Enron MCMC-derived L3 result; M4 MPLE joint score is supplementary only. |
| NHP-D neural reproduction | Not passed | No neural benchmark result is admitted. |
| Chronological analysis | Bounded diagnostic only | No forecasting, STERGM, or RHEM claim belongs to Paper 1. |
